title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Pet and house sitting
audience: Pet and house sitters who want more work from businesses and property managers near them, and who want to contact them lawfully.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a client need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide the stays and visits you want first
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want. Write down the stay types you do well (visits, overnight stays, house sitting), the day rate you can sustain, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each client needs you. A regular stay on a route you already drive is worth far more than a one-off job across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows.

instruction.heading: Score prospects against the criteria
instruction.body: Keep every prospect in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit. Ask whether the prospect is inside your area, has a repeat need, has a person who makes the decision, and needs a service your cover allows. Property managers and businesses that send staff away for long periods are examples to evaluate, but add a prospect only when it passes the criteria. Record the date each entry was added and where its contact details came from. Use only contact details published for business use. Do not buy or harvest lists: ACMA's guidance says buying a list does not remove the need to show consent (ACMA, 28 March 2019; an older source). Whether the Privacy Act applies depends on turnover and other factors, so check the OAIC's small business guidance.

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a need is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely soon. Examples include a public notice of planned building works, a new business opening on a street where you already work, a change of occupier at a site you already serve, or a competitor closing in your area. Use signals to decide when to contact a business, not to build a profile of people. Do not monitor private people, use personal information that is not public, or go to a home to make an offer. Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts (Victorian Government, 7 August 2026). Some councils publish planning permit registers, so check your own council's register.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message says how you came to know about the business, makes one observation you can verify from public view or from the business's own published material, and offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined period or a fifteen-minute call. Keep it short and do not overstate what you know. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found that many approaches were pressured or misleading, and that many salespeople did not identify themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026). An honest message that names you is therefore a practical advantage as well as a compliance step.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart. If a prospect says no or asks you to stop, remove them at once and record the date. Review each month which tier and which signal produced paid work, and move your effort there.

procedure: Write the stay types, area, day rate and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason and a contact source.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each tier, with the source of the contact, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message under the electronic message rules, and against your cover and local rules, before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, follow up on the fixed schedule, and remove anyone who asks you to stop.

workedExamples.situation: A house sitter covers three suburbs. A public notice goes up about planned repairs to the common areas of a block of flats in one of them, and the managing agent's business email is published on the block's contact page. The sitter has no existing link to the agent.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the sitter send a sales message to the agent now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: She should not send a sales email simply because the address is published. ACMA's Spam Act guidance says that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages (ACMA, last updated 28 March 2019; an older source). She checks whether the agent has agreed to receive marketing or has invited contact. If not, she waits for an invitation or uses a route the agent has agreed to. A call to a registered number is limited by the Do Not Call Register rules, so she checks the register first. Any message names the notice, says how she learned of it, offers one specific item she could handle, and asks one question. She does not contact owners or tenants using private details, and she does not enter the common area without an invitation. She offers only the services her cover allows.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for area, stay type and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to every prospect on a broad list
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person gave you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Offering a stay type you are not covered for
commonErrors.prevention: Check your cover and the local rules before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or after a request to stop
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a service in outreach unless your cover and the rules where the work is done allow it. This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority. Victorian rules for in-home pet sitting are UNRESOLVED, so ask the council before you offer that service in Victoria.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. The Spam Act text was not read for this research, so check it before sending.

Public listings and public notices do not by themselves permit contact about anything. OAIC guidance on direct marketing says public information is not exempt from the rules where the Privacy Act applies. Use only contact details published for business use, and stop when someone objects.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned
summary: Define the stays you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should a house sitter contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside the area, because it looks large
A business with several sites inside the area that the sitter already visits
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A holiday-rental manager's business address is published on a website. What does that allow?
options: Nothing by itself; the sender still needs consent or an invitation before a commercial message
Sending any marketing message to that address, since it is public
Calling the number without checking the Do Not Call Register

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending
